title: Area VIII review: Fundamentals of Flight
intro: These questions mix the four Tasks of Area VIII: straight-and-level flight, level turns, climbs and climbing turns, and descents and descending turns. Many join two of them in one first-lessons instructing situation, such as a level-off and retrim after a climb or the rollout from a gliding turn, the way an examiner would ask.

questions.q: On a straight leg, your learner keeps gazing out the left window at the airport, and the airplane slowly drifts left even though she says she is not pushing on the controls. What does the AFH tell you to teach?
options: The propeller's left-turning tendency is the cause in cruise, so she should hold steady right rudder pressure on every straight leg to cancel it fully
The drift means the airplane is out of trim, so she should roll in aileron trim until the drift stops and then keep watching the airport
Fix her eyes on one point on the nose, because the nose's short horizontal line is the primary reference for keeping the wings level
Looking to one side, usually the left from the left seat, narrows the view and puts unconscious pressure on the controls that way; scan both wingtips
questions.why: The AFH says pilots tend to look out to one side continually, generally the left from the left seat. That restricts the angle of view and causes unconscious pressure on the flight controls in that direction, so the pilot should not fixate in one direction. Observing both wingtips is the only positive check for level wings and also brings traffic, terrain and weather into the scan [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. The nose is the wrong primary reference: its short horizontal line lets slight deviations go unnoticed, so the wingtips come first [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. The propeller answer is wrong because the built-in compensation is set for cruise speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. Trimming away a drift that she is causing treats the symptom; a trimmed airplane in smooth air needs almost no control pressure [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

questions.q: Climbing at 750 fpm to 4,500 feet, your learner starts the level-off at 4,425 feet and keeps climb power, as you briefed. Now level at 4,500, the airspeed builds toward cruise. What must she do with pitch while it builds?
options: Hold the first level attitude fixed until cruise speed; with the wings level, a change in airspeed does not change lift, so any pitch change now would only start a descent in the wrong direction
Lower the nose gradually as the speed builds: lift grows with speed, so the angle of attack must come down or the airplane climbs. At cruise speed, set cruise power and retrim
Nothing yet: she should first reduce to cruise power, because climb power at a level attitude overspeeds the engine, then fix pitch
Raise the nose slightly as the speed builds, so the airspeed does not overshoot cruise before she reduces the power to the cruise setting and retrims
questions.why: The level-off lead is 10 percent of the climb rate: 0.10 x 750 = 75 feet, so 4,500 - 75 = 4,425 feet. The AFH then has climb power kept temporarily so the airplane accelerates, and at cruise speed the power is set to cruise and the airplane retrimmed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. While it accelerates, lift rises with speed, so the angle of attack must be decreased, timed with the speed change; too slowly and the airplane climbs, too fast and it descends [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]]. The IFH says the same: constant pitch changes are needed as the airspeed increases [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Pulling power at once is wrong: the AFH keeps climb power so the airplane reaches cruise speed.

questions.q: On a long straight leg your learner alternates 15-second stares at the panel with a quick glance outside, and she never sees the traffic you point out. Which plan fits the sources?
options: Let the long panel stares go, because the eyes refocus at once on a distant object; only slow scanning outside is the problem
Scan outside in wide 30° sweeps of half a second each so the whole sky is covered quickly, and look inside only now and then to keep her head up and her scan moving
Have her fix her eyes on a single distant spot on the horizon, because eyes pick out traffic best when they stay focused in one place
Keep the panel looks brief and scan outside in eye movements of 10° or less, 1 second per area; her eyes need several seconds to refocus from the panel
questions.why: The AFH says effective scanning is a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements of no more than 10°, with each area observed for at least 1 second, and that the eyes may need several seconds to refocus when switching between the panel and distant objects [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Under integrated instruction the panel gets only brief checks, then the pilot returns to the outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. A fixed gaze is wrong: the AFH notes the eyes tend to focus somewhere even in a featureless sky, so glances should be shifted and refocused at intervals [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]. Wide, fast sweeps break both numbers [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

questions.q: In cruise at constant power in a fixed-pitch trainer, your learner looks down at a chart. You hear the wind noise rising and the engine note climbing. What is most likely happening, and what do you teach?
options: The nose has dropped: rising air noise likely means more speed and less pitch, and a fixed-pitch engine sounds higher as pitch decreases. Teach her to react: look out and reset the nose
The power has crept up by itself; she should ease the throttle back until the engine note sounds normal again and leave the pitch attitude where it is
The nose has risen: a rising engine note in a fixed-pitch airplane means the pitch attitude is increasing, so she should lower the nose a little against the horizon and then check the altimeter
Nothing she needs to act on yet: a change in sound in level flight means little, so she should wait until the altimeter or VSI confirms a trend
questions.why: The AFH says rising rushing-air noise likely means airspeed increasing and pitch decreasing, and in a fixed-pitch airplane the engine sound increases as pitch decreases; the instructor teaches perceiving and reacting to these cues, not just noticing them [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]. With power constant, airspeed stays essentially constant in straight-and-level, so a speed change points to pitch, which is corrected against the natural horizon and then cross-checked [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]. The same sound cue is one of the three airspeed references in glides [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Waiting for the altimeter is the habit to break, not teach.

questions.q: On an evening dual flight over water, your learner holds the nose where it looks right against a line of lights on a distant shore, but her picture disagrees with the attitude indicator. The sky is dark and no horizon shows over the water. What is going on, and what do you teach?
options: The leans: she feels banked after an unnoticed turn, so she should lean the other way until the airplane feels level
A good visual picture: lights on the shore are valid horizon references, so she should keep the nose on them and trust the picture over the instrument
Bright lights make the horizon easier to see, so she should lower her seat and keep her eyes on the shoreline to hold the attitude
A false horizon, since shoreline lights can be mistaken for stars; with no visible horizon it is IMC for practical purposes, so use the instruments
questions.why: The PHAK says a false horizon can occur flying toward the shore of an ocean or large lake at night, because the relative darkness of the water lets shoreline lights be mistaken for stars [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]. The AFH says that if no horizon can be seen, for example night over a dark ocean, it is IMC for practical and safety purposes, and attitude is then controlled by the instruments [[24:65|AFH 3-4]]. Integrated instruction does not prepare a learner for IMC, and unless a pilot has many hours of instrument training, flight at night when the horizon is not visible should be avoided [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. The leans come after leveling from a prolonged turn, not from shoreline lights [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

questions.q: You want your learner to fly a standard-rate level turn at 110 knots true airspeed. Using the PHAK rate-of-turn formula, about what bank does it take, and which instrument confirms the rate?
options: About 17°; the turn coordinator, whose second mark shows a standard-rate turn of 3° per second
About 17°; the attitude indicator, whose second bank mark shows standard rate at any airspeed
About 30°; the turn coordinator, whose miniature wing on the second mark shows 30° of bank
About 11°; the turn coordinator, because a faster airplane needs less bank for the same rate of turn
questions.why: Rate of turn equals 1,091 times the tangent of the bank divided by true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. For 3° per second: tan(bank) = 3 x 110 / 1,091 = 0.302, so the bank is about 16.8°, about 17°. The PHAK adds that a higher airspeed needs more bank for the same rate, not less [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. The turn coordinator's second mark shows a standard-rate turn, 3° per second, and it shows only rate and direction of turn, not bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. Set the bank on the cowling and horizon first, then confirm inside [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

questions.q: You script a spoken demonstration of a 30° level turn for your learner, following the AIH sample. Which version matches it?
options: Clear the area, bank, and hold the ailerons deflected until the turn is done; start the rollout on the new heading and keep the back pressure in until the wings are level, then trim
Clear, then bank with no back pressure and use rudder to hold the turn; lead the rollout by the full bank angle, then add power and trim once the wings are level

Clear; power slightly, bank, slight back pressure, rudder into the turn; neutralize the ailerons; lead the rollout by about half the bank, releasing back pressure; at wings level reduce power and trim
Clear, bank and hold some aileron to keep the bank; lead the rollout by half the bank angle; leave the power and trim alone until the next maneuver
questions.why: The AIH sample level turn goes: clear the airspace, add power slightly, bank, apply a slight amount of back pressure and rudder in the direction of the turn, and neutralize the ailerons and trim at the desired bank. Then lead the rollout by about half the bank with coordinated pressures while releasing back pressure, and at wings level reduce power and trim [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. At a medium bank such as 30° the AFH has the ailerons and rudder neutralized, so holding aileron is wrong; the half-bank lead is its rule of thumb, and elevator pressure is relaxed as the bank comes out [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Leading by the full bank or starting on the heading overshoots, and the airplane keeps rolling as long as the ailerons stay deflected [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

questions.q: On her first level turns, your learner rolls in with big, quick aileron and rudder inputs, and by the time she checks pitch and bank the picture has already changed. What does the AFH say, and what does the AIH add about the ailerons?
options: Large, quick inputs are right for beginners, because the airplane's own stability takes out any extra bank once she lets go of the controls
Use small inputs: slower roll rates give time to judge pitch and bank; roll rate follows how far the ailerons move, bank how long they stay moved
Hold the ailerons deflected longer, because the roll rate depends only on how long they are held, not on how far they are moved
Start the turn with rudder alone, the smaller input, since the airplane turns because the nose is yawed toward the turn; the ailerons only join in later
questions.why: The AFH says beginning pilots should not use large aileron and rudder inputs, because those produce rapid roll rates and leave little time to evaluate and correct; smaller inputs give slower roll rates and more time to complete the pitch and bank corrections [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. The AIH adds that the roll rate depends on how much aileron deflection is used, and the steepness of the bank on how long the ailerons are deflected, since the airplane keeps rolling as long as they are [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The rudder does not turn the airplane: the horizontal component of lift does [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. At medium banks the airplane holds its bank rather than returning to level, so it will not remove the extra bank [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

questions.q: Your learner is in a 20° gliding right turn at best glide, turning from 120 to 210. Where should she start the rollout, and which control change avoids the most common problem when returning to a straight glide?
options: At about 190, leading by the full bank angle; and add back pressure as the wings come level so the nose does not drop below the normal glide picture
At about 200, leading by half the bank; and release the extra back pressure held in the turn, or the nose pitches up and the glide speed decays
At about 210, since a gliding turn stops as soon as the ailerons are neutral; then add a little power to bring the glide speed back to best glide
At about 200, leading by half the bank; and hold firm right rudder all through the rollout, since rudder pressures are higher with the power off
questions.why: The turn from 120 to 210 is 90° to the right. The AFH rule of thumb leads the rollout by half the bank: half of 20° is 10°, so start at 200 [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Returning from a gliding turn to a normal glide, the back pressure applied in the turn must be decreased or the airplane may pitch up and lose airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Firm rudder is the tempting wrong answer: with the power off, rudder pedal pressures are reduced, and excessive rudder during recovery from gliding turns is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

questions.q: In a VY climb in a low-wing trainer, your learner says the nose blocks her view ahead. Which advice and which hazard pairing does AC 90-48E give?
options: Hold the climb pitch and rely on ADS-B In, since it shows every aircraft; the worst case is a low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing one
Adjust the pitch attitude to see better over the nose; the worst case is a high-wing airplane flying above a low-wing one
Adjust the pitch attitude to see better over the nose; the worst case is a low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing one
Raise the nose a little more to climb away from any traffic quickly; the worst case is two low-wing airplanes at the same altitude
questions.why: AC 90-48E says pilots can compensate for blind spots in a climb by adjusting the pitch attitude to improve visibility over the nose. It also says high-wing airplanes have restricted visibility above and low-wing airplanes limited visibility below, so the worst case is a low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing airplane [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. ADS-B In helps, but not every aircraft is equipped with ADS-B Out or a transponder, so not all aircraft show on the display [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. The climb attitude itself creates extra blind spots, which is why raising the nose further is the wrong direction [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

questions.q: Your learner will level off at 3,000 feet and stay at the climb airspeed to start the next exercise, instead of accelerating to cruise. Which level-off technique matches the IFH?
options: Lower the nose briskly right at 3,000 feet with no lead, since the airplane stops climbing as soon as the nose comes down
Keep climb power after leveling until the airspeed settles, then reduce power to the cruise setting and retrim for straight-and-level flight at the new altitude
Reduce power first and hold the climb attitude until the vertical speed reads zero, then lower the nose to the level picture
Lower the nose to the level attitude for that airspeed and reduce power at the same time, in step with the pitch change, so the airspeed stays constant
questions.why: The IFH says that to level off at climbing airspeed, lower the nose to the pitch attitude for that airspeed in level flight while reducing power to the setting for that airspeed; if the power comes off in proportion to the pitch change, airspeed stays constant. It also uses a lead of about 10 percent of the vertical speed, because the airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Keeping climb power is the AFH technique for leveling at cruise speed, so the airplane would accelerate past climb speed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

questions.q: From level cruise your learner is about to start a steady 10° climb at 2,400 pounds and asks how much more thrust than drag that takes. What do you tell her?
options: About 41 pounds, since a climb adds only about 1.7 percent of the weight to the drag
About 410 pounds more than drag, 17 percent of the weight, so power has to go in with the pitch change
None: in any steady climb thrust still just equals drag, because lift goes back to its level-flight value
About 2,400 pounds more than drag, the whole weight, as in every climb
questions.why: The PHAK says the thrust needed for a stabilized climb equals drag plus a percentage of the weight that depends on the angle of climb: a 10° climb needs drag plus 17 percent of the weight, and only a climb straight up needs all of it [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. Here that is 0.17 x 2,400 = 408 pounds, about 410. Lift does go back to about its level-flight value once the climb is steady, which is why the 'no extra thrust' answer tempts, but part of the weight now acts along with drag, so thrust must cover it [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. That is why the AFH has climb power added at the same time as the pitch change [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

questions.q: You are checking out a commercial learner in a trainer with a controllable-pitch propeller and cowl flaps. From cruise, which climb entry matches the AFH?
options: Propeller control forward first, then climb power as the nose comes up; set cowl flaps to keep cylinder head temperatures in limits, with right rudder for P-factor and torque
Throttle up first and the propeller control after it, so the engine never runs at high RPM with low manifold pressure; then close the cowl flaps to cut drag and hold right rudder for P-factor
Raise the nose and let the airspeed settle at VY before adding any power, so the propeller governor is not overloaded, and leave the cowl flaps where they were for cruise
Leave the propeller control at the cruise setting and add only throttle, since the propeller control is moved only for takeoff and landing; right rudder as needed
questions.why: The AFH has the straight climb entered by raising the nose to the climb attitude while simultaneously adding climb power; with an independently controllable-pitch propeller, the propeller control is advanced before the engine power is increased. Cowl flaps, if installed, are set to keep cylinder head temperatures within the manufacturer's specifications, and torque and P-factor are countered with right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Throttle first is the tempting wrong answer, but it reverses the AFH order, and closing the cowl flaps works against engine cooling in the climb.

questions.q: Near gross weight, your learner holds VY and watches the VSI sink to 80 fpm and keep falling as she climbs. She asks what the ceilings mean. What do you tell her?
options: Service ceiling is where the airplane cannot climb at all, and at the absolute ceiling it still climbs at 100 fpm, so she can keep going there for a while
She is still below the service ceiling, because the airplane can climb faster than 100 fpm right up to the absolute ceiling at any weight
She is already above the service ceiling (the 100 fpm limit); near the absolute ceiling no excess power is left, VX and VY meet, and the climb rate is zero
VX and VY move farther apart as she climbs, so at height she has a wider choice of climb speeds and more time to react to trouble
questions.why: The PHAK defines the service ceiling as the altitude at which the airplane can no longer climb faster than 100 fpm, so a climb rate of 80 fpm means she is at or above it. At the absolute ceiling there is no excess power, the climb speeds converge and the rate of climb is zero [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. The AFH adds that as altitude increases VX increases and VY decreases until they meet at the absolute ceiling, so they close up rather than spread apart [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. The first answer swaps the two definitions, and the second puts her below a ceiling she has already passed.

questions.q: Your learner flies solid straight-and-level and level turns, and you are planning her first climbs lesson. Which plan fits the AIH?
options: Start with climbing turns in both directions, since they contain a straight climb, and simplify only if she struggles
Build on her level flying and turns, teach straight climbs before climbing turns, and have her master each block before you combine them
Teach straight climbs and climbing turns as one block with no separate practice, since the AIH says blocks of learning should not be broken down
Set aside her level flying and teach climbs as a new subject, since the AIH treats each block of learning as an unrelated subject
questions.why: The AIH says that when a skill relates to previously learned maneuvers, the known to unknown strategy works well, and when teaching more than one skill, starting with the simplest builds confidence and works from simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. It describes blocks of learning that a learner masters individually and then combines, and says the blocks are not isolated subjects but essential parts of the whole [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. The AFH likewise builds each fundamental on the one before, and deficiencies in the earlier ones become barriers later [[24:62|AFH 3-1]]. So climbing turns first, one big block, or an unrelated new subject all fail the AIH advice.

questions.q: For a later lesson, you describe the emergency descent to your learner in a piston trainer. Which description matches the AFH?
options: A high-drag, high-airspeed AFM/POH procedure, such as idle power, gear down and flaps up, often with turns; end practice once stable to avoid over-cooling
A nose-high, power-assisted descent at no more than 1.3 VSO with a steeper-than-normal angle, used mainly to clear obstacles on approach to a short runway
A 500 fpm descent at the cruise power and airspeed in the AFM/POH, the normal way to lose altitude, which can be practiced for as long as needed
A power-off descent at best glide speed with full flaps, which gives the greatest distance for the altitude lost in still air
questions.why: The AFH says an emergency descent is generally a high drag, high airspeed procedure with a specific airplane configuration, such as power to idle, landing gear extended and flaps retracted, at a specific airspeed from the AFM/POH, and it often includes turns [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Once it is established and stable in training, it should be ended, because prolonged practice in a piston airplane can overcool the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. The first option is the minimum safe airspeed descent, the third is the partial power descent, and the fourth is wrong because flaps add drag and cut glide distance [[24:82|AFH 3-21]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

questions.q: Your learner flies good level turns, holding just the back pressure that keeps altitude. In her first 20° gliding turn she uses that same back pressure, and the airspeed creeps above best glide with the nose low. What do you explain?
options: A gliding turn needs less back pressure than a level turn, because with no propeller slipstream the airplane tends to pitch up; she should relax some pressure and let the speed settle back at best glide
She should add a little power in every gliding turn, because no airplane can hold its glide speed in a bank without some thrust to replace the lift used for turning
A gliding turn needs more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn: lift is tilted, light pressures invite too much rudder, and the airplane tends to nose down with the power off
She should steepen the bank to about 30°, where the airplane holds its bank with neutral controls, so the nose stops dropping and the speed goes back to best glide
questions.why: The AFH lists three elements that push the nose down and increase glide speed in a gliding turn: less vertical lift because the lift is tilted, excessive rudder from the reduced control pressures, and the airplane's normal tendency to nose down with the power off. They make it necessary to use more back pressure than in a straight glide or a level turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The instructor should explain why coordination is harder in gliding turns [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Steepening to a medium bank changes only the aileron needed to hold the bank, not the pitch [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

questions.q: You run a simulated engine failure while your learner glides at best glide, descending 1,000 fpm toward a level-off altitude. In the debrief she asks how a real, complete power failure would differ at the end of the glide. What does the AFH say?
options: In practice she holds best glide to the ground; in a real failure she adds power at the 100 foot lead point to soften the landing, then raises the nose
There is no difference: in a real failure she also adds power at the 100 foot lead point and raises the nose, because the engine can supply power whenever she asks for it
In a real failure she should slow below best glide early to stretch the glide toward the field, and in practice she should hold best glide until she is level
In practice, power goes in as the altimeter shows the 10 percent lead, 100 feet above, while she raises the nose; in a real failure she holds best glide until it is time to configure for landing
questions.why: The lead is 10 percent of 1,000 fpm, or 100 feet. For simulated power failure training the AFH has power applied as that lead value appears on the altimeter, which gives a slow but positive power application while the pilot raises the nose to stop the descent and retrims. In a complete power failure the best glide speed is held until it is necessary to reconfigure for landing, with a steeper approach planned and the same 10 percent lead slowing the descent before landing [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Slowing below best glide to stretch the glide is the cardinal-rule error and can lead to landing short or a stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

questions.q: After slow flight practice, your learner sets up best glide toward a field for a simulated engine failure but leaves 10° of flaps down. She holds best glide speed exactly. What does the AFH say about her glide?
options: Flaps make no difference as long as she holds the best glide speed, because the glide ratio depends only on the airspeed flown and not on the configuration
The flaps add lift, so the glide path flattens and she reaches farther than she would with the flaps up; she should leave them down until the field is made, then use full flaps
The added drag needs a lower pitch to hold the speed, so the glide path steepens and the distance shrinks; to glide farthest, retract the drag devices if possible
She should keep the flaps and raise the nose a little below best glide speed to make up for the extra drag, so the glide stretches back to the planned distance
questions.why: The AFH says the highest glide ratio occurs at maximum L/D, so drag-producing items such as flaps, landing gear and cowl flaps matter: more drag needs a lower pitch attitude to hold the airspeed, which steepens the glide path and cuts the distance, so all drag-producing components should be eliminated if possible [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Slowing below best glide to stretch it breaks the AFH cardinal rule and can lead to landing short or a stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

questions.q: From level cruise your learner closes the throttle and holds altitude with back pressure, as in the AFH glide entry. Using the AFH energy rules, what is happening and what comes next?
options: Drag now exceeds thrust, so total energy falls; holding altitude lets the airspeed bleed off, and at best glide speed she pitches down just enough to hold it
Thrust now exceeds drag, so energy builds and the back pressure stores it as altitude; she should add more power so the speed does not rise too far
Altitude and airspeed change in the same direction, so back pressure keeps both at their cruise values until she lowers the nose to descend
Total energy stays the same, because the lost thrust turns into altitude; she can leave the nose where it is and the speed will not change at all
questions.why: With the throttle closed, thrust is less than drag and total mechanical energy decreases. The AFH says the pilot can let the airplane descend at a constant airspeed or slow down while maintaining altitude [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Its rule for less energy is to reduce the throttle and then pitch down just enough to hold the desired speed, so after holding altitude until the speed falls to best glide, she lowers the nose to hold that speed [[24:96|AFH 4-10]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. When energy is traded between altitude and airspeed they always change in opposite directions, so back pressure cannot hold both [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].
